Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
The people responsible have faced no consequences
There is something wrong with me as a person

vignette: Arjun Patel, a forty-nine-year-old South Asian American military medic, stood at his locker in the motor pool, his knuckles white as a police cruiser idled at the gate. The trauma that fractured his life began during the final months of his first marriage, when his then-partner, a corrections officer, used her rank to control his movements in their home. She would return from night shifts drenched in sweat, her body odor sharp and acrid, and when his relatives visited, they watched in silence as she escalated to physical strikes. That night, the scent of her exertion, the presence of his extended family, and the sheer weight of her authority fused into a single, inescapable threat. Since then, any encounter with law enforcement, the familiar faces of his relatives, or the heavy smell of a stranger’s sweat directly drives his avoidance of similar tactical clothes, gyms where instructors sweat heavily, and other people. These sensory and social triggers immediately pull the event back into his consciousness, making the past feel as though it is happening right now rather than as a detached story. The constant exposure to these cues convinces him that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, that the people responsible have faced no accountability, and that there is something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. Because he believes his own nature is defective and justice is impossible, he systematically withdraws, which in turn keeps his nervous system locked in a state of relentless threat monitoring. His negative appraisals directly fuel his hypervigilance; he has difficulty falling asleep because he needs to stay alert, and he only feels safe in a very limited number of places, namely his locked study. His belief that he is broken ensures that the memories return with unmediated force, while his appraisals of lost meaning and no accountability keep his dread unmodulated. The vivid intrusions themselves dictate his avoidance: when the memory returns, he feels physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event, and the nonverbal quality of the recall makes him retreat further because he cannot articulate what happened. These memories sustain his negative appraisals by confirming his fear that he is damaged beyond repair. His reliance on safe zones and sleep vigilance, in turn, dictates his avoidance strategies by making the physical and social world feel too dangerous to navigate. The threat state ensures that the memories return with raw, nonverbal intensity, while his relentless dread convinces him his life is meaningless. His hypervigilance makes ordinary stimuli, like a dropped wrench or a uniformed figure, feel like direct premonitions of danger, which reinforces his avoidance. His avoidance sustains his threat response by limiting corrective experiences, which deepens his negative appraisals, which in turn makes the original triggers feel even more catastrophic. The memories that flood him keep his appraisal of defectiveness active, while his negative beliefs ensure his threat monitoring never downshifts. What finally drove Arjun to seek professional help was a collapse during a mandatory physical fitness assessment at the military base. The smell of his drill instructor’s sweat, combined with the distant wail of a police siren, triggered a full-blown panic attack that left him gasping on the asphalt, his body recognizing the sensory cues as immediate mortal danger even though he is currently married and living in a quiet suburban home. He is most afraid of living the rest of his life trapped in a body that cannot distinguish past from present, but he holds onto a fragile hope that he might finally learn to trust himself again and break the cycle that has kept him isolated from his occupation, his spouse, and his own sense of safety.
